ctx.x: Well what is post bebop vernacular for you?

Particularly, like yesterday we were talking about Coltrane. So I’m thinking more of the hard bop, from the mid-fifties on like Sonny Rollins, Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers, John Coltrane, Joe Henderson, Woody Shaw, Freddie Hubbard, J.J. Johnson. © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

Thinking more in terms of the post — from the mid-fifties on. And of course even now you’ve got so many great young players out here who have learned that part of the language. What I find in my experiences as an educator and as a musician is that again a lot of people who are say forty and under haven’t bothered to get what Kenny Washington called pre-bop. And music before Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie. And I’m thinking of people like Benny Carter, Chu Berry, Fletcher Henderson, all of the great big bands,…

items.title: Steve Wilson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 25, 2002
items.q: You know not in the sense of like well yeah it’s the coming out of a Woody Shaw thing or a Freddy Hubbard thing.

ctx.x: You know not in the sense of like well yeah it’s the coming out of a Woody Shaw thing or a Freddy Hubbard thing. No. But in his own language, in his own syntax. And he played some things that made us all raise our eyebrows, what was that? Where did he find that? How did he pull that out of the air? So we tend to dismiss some of these musicians that we don’t associate with a modern Coltrane era. But I would beg to differ that they are just as relevant as anybody in the modern era.
Plus what you can learn from a guy like Joe from his everyday life and his character.
